title: OpenFlow
text:
The Open Networking Foundation (ONF), a user-led organization dedicated to promotion and adoption of software-defined networking (SDN),[1] manages the OpenFlow standard.[2] ONF defines OpenFlow as the first standard communications interface defined between the control and forwarding layers of an SDN architecture. OpenFlow allows direct access to and manipulation of the forwarding plane of network devices such as switches and routers, both physical and virtual (hypervisor-based). It is the absence of an open interface to the forwarding plane that has led to the characterization of today's networking devices as monolithic, closed, and mainframe-like. A protocol like OpenFlow is needed to move network control out of proprietary network switches and into control software that's open source and locally managed.[3]

A number of network switch and router vendors announced intent to support or are shipping supported switches for OpenFlow, including Alcatel-Lucent,[4] Big Switch Networks,[5] Brocade Communications,[6] and Radisys.[7]

### Development

Version 1.1 of the OpenFlow protocol was released on 28 February 2011, and new development of the standard was managed by the ONF.[8] In December 2011, the ONF board approved OpenFlow version 1.2 and published it in February 2012.[9] The current version of OpenFlow is 1.5.1.[10] However, version 1.6 has been available since September 2016, but accessible only to ONF's members.

In May 2011, Marvell and Larch Networks announced the availability of an OpenFlow-enabled, fully featured switching solution based on Marvell's networking control stack and the Prestera family of packet processors.[11,12]

Indiana University in May 2011 launched a SDN Interoperability Lab in conjunction with the ONF to test how well different vendors' software-defined networking and OpenFlow products work together.[13]

In June 2012, Infoblox released LINC, an open-source OpenFlow version 1.2 and 1.3 compliant software switch.[14]

In February 2012, Big Switch Networks released Project Floodlight, an Apache-licensed open-source software OpenFlow Controller,[15] and announced its OpenFlow-based SDN Suite in November of that year, which contains a commercial controller, and virtual switching and tap monitoring applications.[16]

In February 2012, HP said it is supporting the standard on 16 of its Ethernet switch products.[17]

In April 2012, Google's Urs Hölzle described how the company's internal network had been completely re-designed over the previous two years to run under OpenFlow with substantial efficiency improvement.[18]

In January 2013, NEC unveiled a virtual switch for Microsoft's Windows Server 2012 Hyper-V hypervisor, which is designed to bring OpenFlow-based software-defined networking and network virtualisation to those Microsoft environments.[19]
